title: PSMix: Robust Point Cloud Recognition through Spectral Domain Mixing
claim: Existing mixing methods create geometric discontinuities and unrealistic samples; ours blends two inputs into one smooth, coherent result.
layout: Rows per method, source samples at left and right, mixed outputs between
description: A grid comparing mixed point-cloud samples. A blue airplane (sample A) sits at the lower left and a pink night stand (sample B) at the lower right, each labeled below. Between them, three rows show spatial-domain mixes from existing methods: RSMix, PointCutMix-K and PointCutMix-R. Each row shows two mixed outputs. These look fragmented: pink blocks overlap the plane, points are scattered, and the pieces are visibly cut apart. A dashed line labeled 'Mixed Samples' separates these rows from the bottom row. The bottom row is labeled 'Spectral Domain (ours)' with PSMix in gold. It shows a smooth, blended airplane-like shape and a smooth night stand-like shape. Method names sit in the center column. Blue and pink color coding marks the source of each point. The eye goes first to the large source objects, then down the rows to the clean bottom row.
caption: Comparison of spatial and spectral mixup of point clouds. While spatial methods (top three rows) introduce geometric discontinuities, PSMix (bottom row) leverages spectral interpolation to generate smooth, structurally coherent augmented samples.
abstract: While data augmentation is essential for robust point cloud recognition, conventional spatial mixup strategies often compromise geometric integrity by generating physically unrealistic samples. To overcome this limitation, we propose PSMix, which shifts the mixing paradigm to the spectral domain via the Spherical Harmonic Transform. Instead of simple coordinate interpolation, PSMix performs a rotation-aware hierarchical mixing on spectral coefficients. This approach explicitly preserves global structural properties while diversifying local details, achieving a balance that spatial methods struggle to maintain. Complementing this, we introduce an adversarial rotation optimization strategy to enforce invariance against challenging orientations. Extensive experiments on ModelNet-C and ScanObjectNN-C demonstrate that PSMix achieves state-of-the-art robustness, while also serving as an orthogonal plug-in that further boosts the performance of existing spatial strategies.
